nameStory: The Sea Mullet gets its name from its preferred saltwater habitat along coastlines, distinguishing it from freshwater mullets. The word 'mullet' itself comes from the Latin 'mullus,' referring to the reddish color of some ancient Mediterranean mullet species, though our Sea Mullet is more silvery-gray.
description: The Sea Mullet is a silvery, torpedo-shaped fish that's built for life in coastal waters where salt and fresh water mix. These robust fish typically grow 12 to 30 inches long, with a somewhat flattened head that gives them one of their alternate names - flathead mullet. They're schooling fish that you'll often see in groups, and they're perfectly at home whether the water is salty, brackish, or completely fresh.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Torpedo-shaped body that feels firm and muscular to the touch, with a distinctly flattened head that looks almost squashed from above

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Silvery-gray sides with a darker back, often showing faint horizontal stripes that catch the light when the fish moves

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small, downward-facing mouth positioned below the snout, perfect for bottom-feeding - you can barely fit your pinky finger inside

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Two separate dorsal fins on the back with the front one having sharp spines that feel prickly when handled

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized fish typically 12-30 inches long, heavy for their length and feeling substantial when lifted

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in schools over sandy or muddy bottoms in coastal areas, estuaries, and rivers where they can tolerate changing salinity levels

habitat: In New England, Sea Mullet prefer shallow coastal waters, estuaries, and the lower reaches of rivers where saltwater meets fresh. They're most commonly found over sandy or muddy bottoms in protected bays and harbors. These adaptable fish can handle the changing salinity levels found in tidal areas and salt marshes.

seasonality.spring: Sea Mullet begin moving into estuaries and rivers as waters warm, becoming more active in their feeding behavior over muddy and sandy bottoms.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when schools are most visible in shallow coastal waters and estuaries, actively feeding during daylight hours.
seasonality.fall: Continue feeding heavily in preparation for cooler months, still commonly seen in schools in protected coastal areas.
seasonality.winter: Less active in New England's cold waters, may move to deeper areas or migrate south to warmer regions.

funFact: Sea Mullet are like underwater vacuum cleaners - they actually eat mud and sand, filtering out tiny algae, dead plants, and microscopic creatures, then spit out the leftover sediment through their gills!
confusionNotes: Sea Mullet are most commonly confused with White Mullet, but Sea Mullet have a more flattened head and grow larger. Remember: 'Sea = bigger and flatter head.' Young Sea Mullet might be mistaken for other silvery school fish, but their distinctive downward-pointing mouth is a dead giveaway.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Sea' Mullet, these fish are actually happiest in brackish water where rivers meet the ocean. They're also known by many other names including striped mullet, flathead mullet, and simply 'mullet' - so don't be confused if you hear different names for the same fish in different locations along the coast.
compareHints: Compared to its closest relative the White Mullet, the Sea Mullet grows significantly larger and has a more pronounced flattened head profile. White Mullet typically stay smaller and have a more rounded head shape. Sea Mullet also tend to school in larger, more visible groups in open coastal waters, while White Mullet prefer shallower, more protected areas.

relatedSpecies.distinction: White mullet are smaller and more silvery than their close relative the striped mullet (sea mullet), which grows larger and has distinctive dark horizontal stripes along its sides.
